claims.text: Multilayer interfaces govern resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings.
Multilayer interfaces act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Chemical complexity and lattice mismatch stabilize the interfaces against shear.
Chemical complexity and lattice mismatch reduce defect mobility at the interfaces.
Physical vapor deposition can be used to produce alternating high-entropy-alloy nanolayers with layer thicknesses of 10–50 nm.
The proposed controlled comparison is between a multilayer coating with repeated interfaces and a monolithic coating having the same overall composition.
The coatings would be tested at approximately 600°C in an inert atmosphere under sustained load for several hundred hours.
A high density of chemically and structurally complex interfaces inhibits dislocation glide and climb.
The multilayer interfaces reduce atomic diffusion across layers.
Multilayer interfaces introduce local lattice distortions and energy barriers to defect motion.
Impeded dislocation propagation and retarded diffusion reduce the rate of time-dependent plastic deformation relative to a homogeneous coating.
The multilayer coating will have a lower creep rate or accumulated strain than the monolithic baseline under identical test conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies when temperature and stress activate dislocation motion and diffusion but remain below levels that cause interface degradation or grain growth.
Significant interdiffusion is expected to limit the mechanism's applicable temperature range.
The magnitude of creep reduction depends on lattice mismatch, interface coherence, and layer thickness.
Interface-induced strengthening may compete with stress concentration at interfaces.
Dislocation pile-up at interfaces is an expected microstructural observation if the proposed barrier mechanism operates.
